performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How does the walking theme change when it is played quietly by wind instruments?
intro: After the heavy ox-cart the visitor walks quietly, in woodwinds. A short swell of strings crests in the middle, then the sound thins into the next picture. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

cues.title: Winds, in bars of five, six, seven
cues.text: In Ravel’s scoring the flutes begin, then oboes and bassoons take over the walking. The piano score’s bars run five, six and seven beats, so the stride is less even than in the first Promenade. The level stays gentle, about −14 to −18 dB.
cues.evidence: Flutes, then oboes and bassoons: LA Phil note (Orrin Howard). Five-, six- and seven-beat bars: Lamm’s score (Mutopia, promenade-4.ly). Relative level −13.9, −17.6, −13.4 and −13.1 dB at 0:00, 0:05, 0:10 and 0:15.

cues.title: Mussorgsky in the interludes
cues.text: Writing to Stasov around 12 June 1874, as he reached the fourth number, Mussorgsky said the transitions were good and added: “My physiognomy can be seen in the interludes.” By his own account the Promenades carry his own face.
cues.evidence: Letter to Vladimir Stasov, probably 12 June 1874, quoted in Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (composition history), which also gives Stasov’s account of the Promenade as Mussorgsky roving through the exhibition. The note sits at the start of the movement’s short swell (−13 to −6 dB, 0:15–0:20); the swell itself is described in the join card.

cues.title: A light, quick close
cues.text: The level falls by about fourteen decibels at 0:35 and the attacks pick up again, over three a second, at a much quieter level. The Promenade thins into small, quick figures that lead directly into the next picture.
cues.evidence: Relative level −7.4 dB (0:30), −21.3 (0:35), −23.2 (0:40); onsets per second 1.0 (0:30), 3.4 (0:35). That the Promenade leads into the next movement: Philharmonia guide (“before leading us into the next movement”).

transitions.title: Strings enter and the walk swells
transitions.how: The woodwind walk reaches a point of rest, then blustery strings join and the sound grows to its short peak between 0:20 and 0:30. The pulse is still the unequal walk, but the colour turns from delicate winds to a fuller blend. The crest is brief: the movement is a quiet interlude, not a statement of weight, and it falls away within ten seconds of its peak.
transitions.evidence: Strongest boundary at 0:18 (novelty 1.00); relative level −13.1 dB (0:15) to −6.2 dB (0:20) and −5.3 dB (0:25), then −21.3 dB at 0:35. Strings added to woodwinds: Philharmonia guide.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (0:42; this file is 0:40), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
